items.title: GenerateResourceConfig server capability is dropped by toproto5/toproto6, so Terraform never calls the framework's GenerateResourceConfig RPC
items.where: internal/toproto5/server_capabilities.go:15-25; internal/toproto6/server_capabilities.go:15-25; source of truth internal/fwserver/server_capabilities.go:41-48
items.current: fwserver.(*Server).ServerCapabilities() returns GenerateResourceConfig: true (added in 2ee75aa, 'Enable GenerateResourceConfig server capability', released in 1.19.0 whose CHANGELOG says config generation moved from Terraform core into the framework for Terraform >= 1.14). Both toproto ServerCapabilities converters copy only GetProviderSchemaOptional, MoveResourceState and PlanDestroy, so the tfprotov5/6.ServerCapabilities sent in GetMetadata and GetProviderSchema always carries GenerateResourceConfig=false. Terraform core (internal/terraform/node_resource_plan_instance.go:1191, main branch) calls provider.GenerateResourceConfig only when providerSchema.ServerCapabilities.GenerateResourceConfig is true and otherwise falls back to genconfig.ExtractLegacyConfigFromState, so the framework's GenerateResourceConfig RPC (proto5server/proto6server/fwserver, ~300 lines) never runs in production.
items.replacement: Add `GenerateResourceConfig: fw.GenerateResourceConfig,` to both converters, and add `GenerateResourceConfig: true,` to the 30 expected ServerCapabilities values in proto5server/proto6server TestServerGetMetadata and TestServerGetProviderSchema (they currently encode the dropped flag).
items.why_equivalent: Not a refactor: it changes the protocol response on purpose (false -> true) to match what fwserver already declares and what the 1.19.0 release notes promise.
items.size: about -0/+32 lines (measured: 2 converter lines; 30 subtests fail after the fix until their expectation gains one line)
items.risk: medium: it switches on, for Terraform >= 1.14, a path that has only run in unit tests; also unverified: how terraform-plugin-mux merges this capability for muxed SDKv2+framework providers. Run terraform-provider-corner (and a muxed provider) with an import block and -generate-config-out on Terraform >= 1.14 and compare with the legacy output before release.
items.proof: As stated, plus: the Terraform core gating (node_resource_plan_instance.go:1191 on the main branch) is unverifiable context from a fetched file, not proof. Verifier reproduced: probe fw true -> proto false for both protocols; sandbox fix -> exactly 30 failing subtests, every diff '- GenerateResourceConfig: false / + true'.
items.impact: No user-visible change in generated configuration today: fwserver.GenerateResourceConfig is a transcription of Terraform core's legacy logic meant to have 'no functionality changes' (fwserver/server_generateresourceconfig.go:39-43; CHANGELOG 1.19.0). The defect is that the protocol response contradicts fwserver.ServerCapabilities, so the about 434-line GenerateResourceConfig path (fwserver 192, protoNserver 82, fromproto 98, toproto 62) never runs in production, and the planned replacement of that logic ('will be replaced in a future release') would silently not take effect.
notes: Field audit: every other tfprotov5/6 response field is either set or intentionally unset (UnsafeToUseLegacyTypeSystem, SchemaBlock.Version, SchemaNestedBlock.MinItems/MaxItems); GenerateResourceConfig is the only fwserver field the converters never read.
Git: commit 2ee75aa touched fwserver/server_capabilities.go and its tests but no toproto file.
Area B's auditor reproduced this independently while checking the fwserver side.

items.title: Move the protocol-neutral 587-line ArgumentsData body out of fromproto5/fromproto6 into one shared internal function; keep both fromprotoN.ArgumentsData as 5-line wrappers
items.scope: internal/fromproto5, internal/fromproto6, new internal package (e.g. internal/fromprotocommon) or internal/fwserver
items.where: internal/fromproto5/arguments_data.go:20-608; internal/fromproto6/arguments_data.go:20-608
items.current: Correction to the count: only 3 lines mention tfprotovN (import, doc comment, signature); the 4th line that differs between the twins is the package clause. With the range clause (55) and argument.Unmarshal (81) that makes 6 protocol-touching lines.
items.replacement: Create `func ArgumentsData(ctx context.Context, numArguments int, unmarshal func(position int, typ tftypes.Type) (tftypes.Value, error), definition function.Definition) (function.ArgumentsData, *function.FuncError)` in a protocol-neutral internal package (the draft uses a new internal/fromprotocommon; internal/fwserver, already imported by fromproto5/6, also works; internal/fwfunction does not, because `function` imports it). Its body is the current body with len(arguments) -> numArguments (6 sites), the range clause -> `for position := range numArguments`, and `argument.Unmarshal(t)` -> `unmarshal(position, t)`. fromprotoN.ArgumentsData keeps its signature: `unmarshal := func(position int, typ tftypes.Type) (tftypes.Value, error) { return arguments[position].Unmarshal(typ) }; return fromprotocommon.ArgumentsData(ctx, len(arguments), unmarshal, definition)`. Protocol-specific lines that must stay per protocol: the []*tfprotovN.DynamicValue parameter and the `arguments[position].Unmarshal(typ)` call.
items.why_equivalent: A move plus parameterisation: statement order, every FuncError text, every logging.FrameworkTrace call and every return value are unchanged. The wrapper reads len(arguments) once and the slice is never mutated, so numArguments equals each former len(arguments); arguments[position] is read at the point where the range variable was used. A callback is used on purpose instead of a generic `T interface{ Unmarshal(tftypes.Type) (tftypes.Value, error) }`: a probe showed that calling a value-receiver method through a type parameter turns the nil-element panic 'runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference' into 'value method ... called using nil *DynamicValue pointer'. The callback keeps the direct call in protocol code, so even that panic text is identical. Only the @caller file:line metadata of the 6 trace log entries changes, as it does for any edit.
items.size: +627/-1178 physical lines (net -551), measured with git diff --no-index --numstat on the author's drafts (fromproto5 +5/-589, fromproto6 +5/-589, core +611, doc.go +6) and matching the author's own A2_argumentsdata.diff; the stated '-1084/+573 (net -511)' is a non-blank-line count (1110 -> 599).
items.risk: low: internal packages only, mechanical, existing tests unchanged. Design note: it would be the first package shared across the deliberately twinned fromproto5/6 packages; internal/fwserver is a cycle-free alternative home (verified).
items.proof: Pinned by TestArgumentsData and TestArgumentsData_ParameterValidators in both fromproto5 and fromproto6 (200 subtests), TestCallFunctionRequest, and TestServerCallFunction in proto5server/proto6server. In a sandbox copy: go build ./internal/..., go vet, go test ./internal/fromproto5 ./internal/fromproto6 and go test -run CallFunction ./internal/proto5server ./internal/proto6server pass unchanged; golangci-lint with the project .golangci.yml on the three packages reports 0 issues. items.title: Replace the 12 copy-pasted ParameterWith<Type>Validators loops in ArgumentsData with one generic helper
items.scope: ArgumentsData core (after A2), or both fromproto5/6 twins if A2 is not taken
items.where: internal/fromproto5/arguments_data.go:162-559; internal/fromproto6/arguments_data.go:162-559
items.current: Addendum: the 12 blocks are identical except a local variable name in the List case (listValue vs listValuable), which has no behavioural effect.
items.replacement: `func runParameterValidators[Valuable, Value, Validator any](ctx, pos int64, attrValue attr.Value, validators []Validator, valuableName string, toValue func(Valuable, context.Context) (Value, diag.Diagnostics), validate func(context.Context, Validator, Value) *function.FuncError) *function.FuncError` holding the loop once. Each case becomes `funcError = function.ConcatFuncErrors(funcError, runParameterValidators(ctx, pos, attrValue, p.GetValidators(), "basetypes.BoolValuable", basetypes.BoolValuable.ToBoolValue, func(ctx context.Context, v function.BoolParameterValidator, value basetypes.BoolValue) *function.FuncError { resp := &function.BoolParameterValidatorResponse{}; v.ValidateParameterBool(ctx, function.BoolParameterValidatorRequest{ArgumentPosition: pos, Value: value}, resp); return resp.Error }))`.
items.why_equivalent: Same case order (first matching interface still wins), same per-validator steps and texts (the valuable name strings match all 12 originals, verified by grep), same validator request values. The type assertion to a type-parameter interface has the same semantics as the explicit one. The only structural change is accumulating into a local FuncError and concatenating once. function.ConcatFuncErrors is associative: it joins non-empty Text with \n and keeps the first non-nil FunctionArgument, so Concat(F, Concat(e1..en)) equals Concat(...Concat(F, e1)..., en) in Text and FunctionArgument. The validate callback returns *function.FuncError, not error, so a nil response error cannot become a non-nil interface.
items.size: +135/-384 on the shared core (net -249), measured with numstat (the author's A3_validators.diff agrees); stated '-372/+128 (net -244)'. Twice that if applied to both twins without A2.
items.risk: low-medium: behaviour is pinned by tests, but it introduces a 3-type-parameter generic plus 12 closures; maintainers may prefer the explicit form
items.proof: TestArgumentsData_ParameterValidators (about 50 cases per package, covering every type, the wrong-Valuable path and validator errors) and TestArgumentsData pass unchanged on the sandbox draft; golangci-lint (project config): 0 issues; gofmt clean. Draft: drafts/A/drafts/A3_fromprotocommon_arguments_data_validators.go; diff: drafts/A/A3_validators.diff.
notes: Independent of A2 in principle, but much cheaper after it (one copy instead of two).

items.title: proto5server/proto6server keep every RPC's cancel func and context chain until StopProvider: unbounded growth per RPC
items.where: internal/proto5server/serve.go:19-39; internal/proto6server/serve.go:19-39; registerContext is called by 27 handlers in proto5server and 35 in proto6server (the stated 29/37 also count the definition line and serve_test.go).
items.current: registerContext appends the context.WithCancel cancel func of every RPC to s.contextCancels. The slice is cleared only by cancelRegisteredContexts, called from StopProvider, which Terraform sends only on interrupt. Each closure keeps its cancelCtx alive, and through it the parent chain (gRPC stream context, terraform-plugin-go logger contexts). terraform-plugin-go's own stoppableContext (tf5server/server.go:441-452) avoids this by using a goroutine that exits when the request context is done.
items.replacement: Make the registry forget completed RPCs: store the cancel funcs in a map[uint64]context.CancelFunc (or a set) and register `context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() { lock; delete(s.contextCancels, id) })` in registerContext. cancelRegisteredContexts keeps iterating and canceling, then resets the map. Draft: drafts/A/drafts/A5_proto6server_serve.go.
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix, not a refactor. StopProvider still cancels every in-flight context. Correction: it is not 'no regression' in every case: when the parent context is never canceled (direct ProviderServer callers passing context.Background()), the draft retains 624 B per RPC instead of 106 B, still until StopProvider. Register the AfterFunc only when in.Done() != nil to keep that case at today's cost.
items.size: +19/-2 per package measured on the v6 draft (+38/-4 total); stated '-2/+15'.
items.risk: medium: touches concurrency in the hot path of every RPC; covered by TestServerCancelInFlightContexts (passes under -race on the draft) and a new growth test
items.proof: Verifier: registry len 1000 (pristine) vs 0 (draft) after 1000 completed RPCs; real-stack heap delta 11,528 vs 2-3 bytes/RPC; -race stress clean; in-flight cancellation preserved. Add first: the growth test (N RPCs with canceled parents, assert empty registry).
items.impact: Measured on the real stack (grpc-go server + tf6server + framework, loopback TCP): about 11.5 KB retained per completed RPC (219.9 MiB per 20,000 GetMetadata RPCs), about 23 times the stated 0.5 KB lower bound, released only by StopProvider or process exit. Each Terraform walk keeps one provider process and sends several RPCs per resource (estimate: about 3 in a plan), i.e. on the order of 35 KB per managed resource, hundreds of MB for workspaces with 10k resources.
notes: Rejected alternative: delete registerContext and rely on terraform-plugin-go's stoppableContext. That is not equivalent for callers that use the ProviderServer directly (providerserver.NewProtocol5/6 consumers, mux, tests); TestServerCancelInFlightContexts pins the framework's own cancellation.

items.title: InvokeAction: if the event stream consumer stops, the provider's Invoke blocks forever in SendProgress (goroutine leak)
items.where: internal/proto5server/server_invokeaction.go:85-88; internal/proto6server/server_invokeaction.go:85-88; internal/fwserver/server_invokeaction.go:37-41
items.current: The Events iterator runs fwserver.InvokeAction in a goroutine and relays progress from the unbuffered fwResp.ProgressEvents channel. When push returns false, the iterator returns and nobody receives from the channel again. push returns false whenever tf5/6server's range loop exits: on ctx.Done (StopProvider or cancellation) or a Send error. SendProgress (`r.ProgressEvents <- ...`, no select) then blocks forever. The provider's Invoke never returns and its cleanup never runs, even if it watches ctx.
items.replacement: In the progress case, before returning on !push, start a drain: `go func() { for { select { case <-fwResp.ProgressEvents: case <-completedChan: return } } }()`. Draft: drafts/A/drafts/A6_proto6server_server_invokeaction.go. A fwserver-side alternative is to make SendProgress select on a done channel.
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix. The normal path (consumer keeps reading) is unchanged: the drain starts only after push has returned false, and then no further events can be delivered anyway.
items.size: +14/-0 per package measured on the v6 draft (+28 total); stated +13.
items.risk: low: only runs after the consumer has gone away
items.proof: Probe (sandbox): an action whose Invoke sends 3 progress events, consumed by a push that returns false after the first event. Today Invoke is still blocked 2 s later; with the draft it returns at once and TestServerInvokeAction still passes. Add first: that probe as a regression test in both packages.
items.impact: Precise trigger: at least one SendProgress after the push that returned false, i.e. two or more progress events after a cancel, or any event after a Send error. Code before the blocking call runs; code after it and Invoke's deferred cleanup never run, and the goroutine leaks until the provider process exits (normally at the end of the Terraform command).

items.title: Drift: toproto5.GetProviderSchemaResponse does not return after a list resource schema conversion error (toproto6 and every other loop do)
items.where: internal/toproto5/getproviderschema.go:121-131 (vs internal/toproto6/getproviderschema.go:118-130)
items.current: All six other loops (provider, provider_meta, action, data source, resource, ephemeral resource), and the same loop in toproto6, append the 'Error converting ... schema' diagnostic and `return protov5`. The v5 list-resource loop only appends, so it keeps converting, emits one diagnostic per failing list resource, and then also runs the state-store check. Both files came from the same commit (ca23057) and v5 never had the return.
items.replacement: Add `return protov5` (after a blank line) inside the `if err != nil` block, as in toproto6.
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix. Only the error path changes, to match toproto6 and the sibling loops (a single diagnostic, then return).
items.size: about -0/+2 lines (trivial)

items.title: ListResource passes a typed-nil *resourceschema.Schema to the provider when RawV5/RawV6Schemas returns an identity schema but no resource schema; NewListResult then panics
items.where: internal/proto5server/server_listresource.go:67-84; internal/proto6server/server_listresource.go:67-83; internal/fromproto5/resource_schema.go:20-23; internal/fromproto6/resource_schema.go:20-23
items.current: The guard checks only `schemaResp.ProtoV6IdentitySchema != nil` and then assigns `req.ResourceSchema, err = fromproto6.ResourceSchema(ctx, schemaResp.ProtoV6Schema)`. For a nil schema (or nil Block) that returns (nil *resourceschema.Schema, nil), which stored in the fwschema.Schema field is a non-nil interface. The v5 comment claims 'There's validation in ListResources that ensures both are set if either is provided'. That is not true: fwserver/server_listresources.go:98-110 validates only when no managed resource of that type exists, and accepts either a complete v5 pair or a complete v6 pair.
items.replacement: Check the converted schema, not only the raw pointers: after fromprotoN.ResourceSchema (and IdentitySchema), treat a nil result (nil raw schema OR nil Block) as a partial pair, i.e. return a 'Converting Resource Schema' diagnostic (or fall back to the framework schemas), and correct the v5 comment. The proposed `ProtoV6Schema != nil && ProtoV6IdentitySchema != nil` guard alone still panics for a schema with a nil Block (reproduced).
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix. Only misconfigured raw schemas (partial pair, or a schema without a Block) change, from a panic to a diagnostic or the framework schemas.
items.size: about -2/+2 lines per package plus about 60 lines of new test (estimated)
items.proof: Probe (sandbox proto6server test): a list resource implementing RawV6Schemas with only ProtoV6IdentitySchema, plus a framework managed resource of the same type, makes the provider's List see req.ResourceSchema != nil, and req.NewListResult panics with 'value method .../resource/schema.Schema.Type called using nil *Schema pointer'. No proto5server/proto6server test exercises the raw-schema branch at all (grep for RawV5Schemas/RawV6Schemas/ProtoV6IdentitySchema in *_test.go finds only fwserver/server_getmetadata_test.go); add one first.

items.title: Schema conversion errors depend on map iteration order: the same invalid schema produces a different diagnostic (and different partial response) on each run
items.scope: internal/toproto5, internal/toproto6 (schema.go, block.go, schema_attribute.go, identity_schema.go, getproviderschema.go, getresourceidentityschemas.go); internal/fromproto5/6 resource_schema.go object attribute types
items.where: Drop internal/fromproto5/resource_schema.go:136 and internal/fromproto6/resource_schema.go:191: their only error, basetypes.TerraformTypeToFrameworkType's 'unsupported tftypes.Type detected', is unreachable (all 9 tftypes kinds are handled and tftypes.Type has unexported methods, so no other implementation can exist). Keep them only as consistency changes if at all.
items.current: Each loop ranges over a map and returns on the first conversion error, so when two or more entries are invalid, the reported attribute, block or resource (and, in GetProviderSchemaResponse, which entries already made it into the maps) depends on Go's randomised map order. Success-path output is deterministic, because the slices are sorted afterwards and the maps are unordered anyway.
items.replacement: Iterate keys in sorted order: `attributes := s.GetAttributes(); for _, name := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(attributes)) { attr := attributes[name]; ... }`. Call GetAttributes()/GetBlocks() once, because some schema types build a new map on each call. The post-loop sort.Slice calls then become no-ops and can be deleted (this also supersedes A14).
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix, but success-path output is byte-identical: names are unique map keys and equal the Name/TypeName fields the old sorts used, so sorted iteration yields the same slice order. Nil versus empty slices are unchanged (same `var x []T` plus append). Only the error path becomes deterministic (first invalid name in sort order).
items.size: +53/-92 measured with numstat on the 6 toproto6 draft files (stated '-74/+47'); with toproto5 about +100/-170 in total (estimated).
items.risk: low: success outputs unchanged (all toproto6 and proto6server tests pass on the draft)
items.proof: Probe: toproto6.Schema on 8 invalid attributes returned 8 distinct error messages over 200 calls; GetProviderSchemaResponse with 5 invalid resource schemas produced 5 distinct outcomes. With the toproto6 draft (drafts/A/drafts/A10_sorted_iteration_toproto6, diff drafts/A/A10_toproto6_sorted.diff): 1 distinct outcome each, and go test ./internal/toproto6 ./internal/proto6server pass.
items.impact: Diagnostics for invalid provider schemas are non-deterministic, which makes provider-side tests of schema errors flaky and repeated runs confusing. No effect on valid schemas.
notes: Do A7 first (or together): A7 changes the same v5 loop.

The same map-order effect also decides the order of separate diagnostics in internal/reflect (Map, FromMap, Struct, FromStruct), map/object semantic equality, every schema ValidateImplementation, privatestate, the GetMetadata lists and PlanResourceChange traces (areas B and C). diag.Diagnostics documents its order as unreliable, so only the cases where order changes a single diagnostic's text are filed: A10 and C5.

items.title: NullifyWriteOnlyAttributes and MarkComputedNilsAsUnknown re-wrap the captured context for every visited value: O(n) retained heap per transform and O(n^2) time with SDK logging on
items.where: internal/fwserver/write_only_nullification.go:24; internal/fwserver/server_planresourcechange.go:416
items.current: Inside the tftypes.Transform callback, `ctx = logging.FrameworkWithAttributePath(ctx, path.String())` assigns to the enclosing function's captured ctx, so each call wraps the previous call's context (a context.WithValue layer holding a copied LoggerOpts per value node). Lookups of other context keys, such as the SDK logger on every log call, walk the whole chain.
items.replacement: `ctx := logging.FrameworkWithAttributePath(ctx, path.String())` at both sites (shadow instead of assign).
items.why_equivalent: Output-preserving: FrameworkWithAttributePath only sets KeyAttributePath, which every call overwrites, so each log line carries the same fields; nothing else reads the accumulated context, and the returned values do not depend on ctx. Verified with tfsdklogtest JSON (list-nested, map, dynamic, block, write-only and computed attributes plus a pre-existing tf_attribute_path field): the same multiset of log lines and equal transformed values in 6/6 runs. The line order is nondeterministic run to run in BOTH variants (tftypes.Transform iterates maps), so compare sorted lines, not bytes.
items.size: 2 lines in 2 files (measured)
items.proof: Verifier benchmark on the real functions (drafts/V-B2/zz_vb2_ctx_test.go.txt in drafts/V-B2/repo vs drafts/V-B2/repo-ctx): logging on, n=8000: NullifyWriteOnlyAttributes 4.16 s vs 0.12 s, MarkComputedNilsAsUnknown 15.2 s vs 0.18 s (quadratic: x3-x6 per doubling); logging off: no measurable time difference, 25.6 MB vs ~0 KB retained while the transform runs. Author's figures (3.72 s vs 0.16 s) reproduce in kind. fwserver/proto5server/proto6server pass with the change (drafts/B2/drafts/fixes).
items.impact: Every managed resource RPC response goes through NullifyWriteOnlyAttributes (Plan, Create, Read, Update, Import, Upgrade, Move); with TF_LOG=trace or debug, large nested states make each RPC quadratically slower, and without logging the transform keeps about 800 bytes per value node alive.
notes: Performance defect with identical output; it can also be reviewed as a refactor because the logs and values are byte-identical.

Repo-wide only these two closures reassign a captured ctx (grep -rn -B3 'ctx = logging.FrameworkWith' --include=*.go . | grep -v _test: the other 5 hits reassign a function parameter at function scope, which is fine).

items.where: resource|datasource|provider|ephemeral|action|list|statestore single_nested_attribute.go and 6 single_nested_block.go GetNestedObject (lines as cited); internal/fwserver/attribute_validation.go:182 (AttributeValidateObject; cited :181) + :191 -> :1118-1155 (null/unknown return at :1139); internal/fwserver/block_validation.go:44 (cited :43) + :123-155 (no null/unknown guard)
items.current: GetNestedObject() copies the attribute's Validators into the synthesized NestedAttributeObject/NestedBlockObject. fwserver.AttributeValidate runs attribute.ObjectValidators() and then, for NestingModeSingle, NestedAttributeObjectValidate runs nestedObject.ObjectValidators(), which is the same slice. BlockValidate does the same. PlanModifiers are not copied, so plan modifiers run once.
items.replacement: Preferred (internal only): in the NestingModeSingle branches of fwserver.AttributeValidateNestedAttributes and fwserver.BlockValidate, skip the nested object's object-level validator loop (e.g. split NestedAttributeObjectValidate/NestedBlockObjectValidate into a validators part and a children part and call only the children part for single nesting). Alternative: drop the Validators line from the 13 GetNestedObject methods, which changes the value returned by an exported method and needs a changelog note.
items.why_equivalent: Behaviour change by design (bug fix): each validator runs once. Visible diagnostics are normally unchanged because diag.Diagnostics.Append already drops the identical second copy.
items.size: about -4/+16 lines in internal/fwserver/attribute_validation.go and block_validation.go (measured on a verifier draft: drafts/V-D/d3/fix.diff) plus 2 tests
items.risk: low: visible output normally identical; coordinate with area B (plan modification and validation), which owns internal/fwserver
items.proof: Overlay-added test (drafts/D/drafts/D-snvalid/zz_probe_test.go; go test -overlay=drafts/D/drafts/D-snvalid/overlay.json -run TestZZProbe -v ./internal/fwserver/) with a counting validator.Object: 'single nested attribute: object validator invoked 2 time(s); diagnostics=1', control 'list nested attribute: invoked 1 time(s)', 'single nested block: invoked 2 time(s); diagnostics=1'. No existing test counts invocations. Add first: a counting-validator test in internal/fwserver/attribute_validation_test.go and block_validation_test.go asserting exactly 1 call.
items.impact: An object validator on a single nested attribute runs twice when the configured object is known and the validator (and earlier checks on that attribute) produced no error. On a single nested block it runs twice whenever it produced no error, including null and unknown blocks. A validator that returns an error runs once. Deterministic diagnostics are deduplicated by Append; non-deterministic ones (counters, timestamps) show up twice.
notes: Cross-area: the execution site is internal/fwserver (area B (plan modification and validation)); the cause is the schema packages' GetNestedObject (area D).
provider/metaschema has no validators, so it is unaffected.

Keep the existing early return on resp.Diagnostics.HasError() unchanged: it already prevents the second run for error validators, and it also suppresses child validation after a parent error. That is area B (plan modification and validation) behaviour, out of scope for this fix.
The area B verifier independently reproduced the double run (2 calls per validation for known values, and for a null block) without knowing about this item.

items.title: Path.Equal and Expression.Equal are asymmetric for zero-value (nil steps) vs empty steps
items.where: path/path.go:105-120; path/expression.go:150-169; affected callers: resource/import_state.go:104,129,137; diag/with_path.go:27; path/paths.go:34,53; path/expressions.go:35,66
items.current: if p.steps == nil && o.steps == nil { return true }; if p.steps == nil { return false }; return p.steps.Equal(o.steps) (Expression adds a root check first). PathSteps.Equal is length-based, so: path.Path{}.Equal(path.Empty()) == false but path.Empty().Equal(path.Path{}) == true; zero.Equal(zero.Copy()) == false (Copy turns nil steps into empty); Expression{}.Equal(path.MatchRelative()) == false, reverse true. Consequences (all reproduced): ImportStatePassthroughID(ctx, path.Path{}, ...) skips its "Resource Import Passthrough Missing Attribute Path" guard and fails later with "Value Conversion Error" (same for both guards in ImportStatePassthroughWithIdentity); Diagnostics.Append keeps both of two otherwise-identical attribute diagnostics whose paths are Path{} and Empty() in one order and dedups them in the other; Paths.String does not skip a zero-value Path although its doc says empty paths are skipped; Paths/Expressions.Contains are order-dependent.
items.replacement: func (p Path) Equal(o Path) bool { return p.steps.Equal(o.steps) } and func (e Expression) Equal(o Expression) bool { return e.root == o.root && e.steps.Equal(o.steps) }
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix. Results change only when the RECEIVER has nil steps and the argument has empty non-nil steps (false -> true); the reverse direction already returned true. Verified on a 425-pair before/after matrix: 10 rows change, all of that kind; every other result is identical. Nothing in the framework distinguishes nil from empty steps (Steps(), String(), Expression(), ParentPath(), totftypes.AttributePath all treat both as the empty path).
items.size: about -30/+2 lines in 2 files (measured on draft3: path.go -13/+1, expression.go -17/+1) plus new test cases
items.risk: low: semantic change limited to zero-value Path/Expression comparisons; all path, diag, tfsdk, internal/fwserver, internal/fwschemadata, internal/fwschema tests pass with the fix (draft3).
items.proof: No test covers nil-vs-empty today (TestPathEqual/TestExpressionEqual only use constructed values). Probe drafts/E/probe/pathequal shows the asymmetry and the ImportStatePassthroughID diagnostic before, and the symmetric results after (probe3 against draft3). Add: TestPathEqual cases zero-empty, empty-zero, zero-copy; TestExpressionEqual zero-relative; a diag Append order test; an ImportStatePassthroughID test with path.Path{}.
items.impact: Equal violates symmetry and the Copy contract; provider code passing an uninitialised path.Path gets a misleading conversion error instead of the intended guard diagnostic, and diagnostic de-duplication depends on append order. Wrong output, no crash.
notes: Fixing Copy() to preserve nil instead would not fix Path{} vs path.Empty().
internal/fwserver NormaliseRequiresReplace (outside area) dedups with Path.Equal after sorting by String; it inherits the fix.

Add: every user-visible consequence needs provider code to pass a zero-value path.Path/Expression (legal Go zero value; the framework never builds one), so tier 2 is the ceiling and tier 3 would also be defensible. The resource package has no test files: the ImportStatePassthroughID/WithIdentity guards are untested today.

items.current: Set calls s.data() (value receiver) through the pointer, so a nil *ResourceIdentity / *Resource panics with "invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference". Reachable: resource Create/Read/Update/Delete/ModifyPlan/ImportState responses carry Identity *tfsdk.ResourceIdentity that the server leaves nil when the resource has no identity schema (internal/fwserver/server_createresource.go:104-123), and list.ListResult.Resource is a *tfsdk.Resource that is nil when a ListResult is built as a literal. resp.Identity.SetAttribute(...) returns the friendly diagnostic; resp.Identity.Set(ctx, &model) crashes the provider.
items.replacement: Add the same nil guard at the top of both Set methods, returning an error diagnostic with the same summary as the sibling SetAttribute guard ("Missing Identity Definition" / "Missing Resource Definition") and a detail that says "set the resource identity" / "set the resource".
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix. Non-nil receivers are unaffected (the guard is a nil check before the existing body); only the nil case changes from a runtime panic to an error diagnostic, matching SetAttribute.
items.size: about -0/+20 lines in 2 files (10 per file, measured) plus 2 test cases
items.risk: low: only the previously-panicking path changes. tfsdk and list package tests pass with the guard (draft3).
items.proof: Probe: (*ResourceIdentity)(nil).SetAttribute -> 'Missing Identity Definition'; .Set -> nil pointer dereference; same pair for *Resource. End to end: providerserver.NewProtocol6WithError + ApplyResourceChange, resource without identity schema, Create calls resp.Identity.Set -> plugin process crashes (SIGSEGV, exit 2); with the guard -> ERROR diagnostic, normal return. No test covers either existing guard (grep in tfsdk tests: 0); add nil-receiver cases to TestResourceIdentitySet/TestResourceSet and the SetAttribute tests.
items.impact: A provider bug (calling resp.Identity.Set on a resource without an identity schema) crashes the plugin process instead of producing the diagnostic that SetAttribute already gives.
notes: By the rubric's letter this is a crash (tier 1), but it is only reachable through provider misuse (no identity schema, or a ListResult literal); the framework already treats the same misuse via SetAttribute as worth a diagnostic, so tier 2.
Get/GetAttribute have value receivers and cannot be guarded the same way; out of scope.

items.title: ObjectValue.Equal returns true for null/unknown objects with different attribute types
items.where: types/basetypes/object_value.go:300-352
items.current: Equal compares state first and returns true for two null (or two unknown) objects before comparing attributeTypes, so NewObjectNull({a: String}).Equal(NewObjectNull({b: Bool})) == true even though their Type()s are unequal. Its own doc says it requires "the same value state, and ... exactly the same attribute types/values", the attr.Value.Equal contract asks for type and value equivalence, and List/Map/Set/Tuple all compare element types before state (their null values with different element types are unequal).
items.replacement: Move the attributeTypes length/key/Equal loop above the state comparison (same order as TupleValue.Equal).
items.why_equivalent: Bug fix, not equivalent: results change only for null/unknown objects whose attribute types differ (true -> false), but those results feed plan modifiers (RequiresReplace/RequiresReplaceIf via PlanValue.Equal(StateValue)), so plan outcomes can change. Known objects already compared types.
items.size: about -8/+8 lines (a block move; measured on draft3) plus test cases
items.risk: medium: Equal results flip (true -> false) for null/unknown objects with different attribute types, and that flips built-in replace planning: dynamicplanmodifier.RequiresReplaceIf and objectplanmodifier.RequiresReplace start requiring replacement when a null/unknown object's attribute types change between state and plan (e.g. a dynamic attribute whose object shape changed); downstream comparisons against types.ObjectNull(nil) also change. Framework suites pass but none covers the case.
items.proof: TestObjectValueEqual has null-null/unknown-unknown cases only with identical attribute types. Probe drafts/E/probe/objequal: ObjectNull(a).Equal(ObjectNull(b)) = true while ListNull/MapNull/SetNull/TupleNull with different element types are false; after the draft fix the object case is false. Add the two different-type cases.
items.impact: Equality is not type-aware for null/unknown objects, unlike every other collection type; latent wrong comparisons in provider code and plan logic that rely on Equal implying identical types.
notes: If maintainers consider the lenient behaviour intended, fix the doc comment instead; either way code and doc disagree today.
Needs a CHANGELOG bug-fix entry because provider-visible Equal results change.

Add: Terraform's own cty treats typed nulls as Equal regardless of type (Equals; RawEquals does not), so the lenient behaviour may be intended; present both options to maintainers (fix the code with a CHANGELOG breaking-behaviour note and replace-planning tests, or fix the doc to say attribute types are compared only for known values, which is zero risk).

Verifier caveat: The code/doc/sibling inconsistency is confirmed, but that the current behaviour is wrong is not demonstrable (cty precedent; no wrong user-visible outcome shown for today's code), and the proposed fix changes replace planning in built-in plan modifiers, which the finding's risk text does not mention.

items.title: ListReturn/SetReturn/MapReturn.NewResultData ignore the CustomType's element type: a CustomType-only collection return crashes the provider on every Run error
items.where: function/list_return.go:59-69; function/set_return.go:59-69; function/map_return.go:59-69; caller internal/fwserver/server_callfunction.go:34; crash site internal/toproto6/function.go:104 (twin internal/toproto5/function.go) -> types/basetypes/list_value.go:225
items.current: NewResultData builds the unknown placeholder from the ElementType field (value := basetypes.NewListUnknown(r.ElementType)) even when CustomType is set, then wraps it with CustomType.ValueFromList. The type docs say 'Either the ElementType or CustomType field must be set' (list_return.go:22, set_return.go:22, map_return.go:22), and the repo's own tests build ListReturn{CustomType: testtypes.ListType{...}} without ElementType. With CustomType only, the placeholder has a nil element type. fwserver.CallFunction always copies runResp.Result into the response, and toproto5/6.FunctionResultData always calls attrValue.ToTerraformValue, which dereferences the nil element type.
items.replacement: In the CustomType branch of the three methods, take the element type from the custom type when ElementType is unset: 'elementType := r.ElementType; if elementType == nil { if t, ok := r.CustomType.(attr.TypeWithElementType); ok { elementType = t.ElementType() } }; valuable, diags := r.CustomType.ValueFromList(ctx, basetypes.NewListUnknown(elementType))' (ValueFromSet/ValueFromMap and NewSetUnknown/NewMapUnknown in the twins). The CustomType == nil branch keeps NewListUnknown(r.ElementType).
items.why_equivalent: This is a bug fix, not a refactor. Nothing changes when CustomType is nil or ElementType is set, because the guard only runs when ElementType is nil. For a CustomType-only return, the placeholder now has the element type the function advertises to Terraform (GetType returns CustomType). The schema path already does this through CustomType.ValueFromTerraform. A custom type that does not implement attr.TypeWithElementType behaves exactly as it does today.
items.size: Author's draft measured exactly -12/+36 (-4/+12 per file). A tighter draft that only reassigns value when ElementType is nil is +24/-0 (8 lines per file including a 2-line comment) with identical probe results. Tests about +120 (estimated).

items.proof: End-to-end reproduction through providerserver.NewProtocol5WithError/NewProtocol6WithError and CallFunction (probe in drafts/F/probe-listreturn). The return is ListReturn, SetReturn or MapReturn with CustomType set to a type that embeds basetypes.ListType/SetType/MapType{ElemType: String}, and Run only sets resp.Error = function.NewFuncError("boom"). Both protocols panic with 'invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference' (stack: basetypes.ListValue.ToTerraformValue list_value.go:225 <- toproto6.FunctionResultData function.go:104 <- toproto6.CallFunctionResponse callfunction.go:22 <- proto6server.CallFunction server_callfunction.go:54). With ElementType also set, the call returns the clean error 'boom'. With a type built like internal/testing/testtypes.ListType (embedding, no overrides), ResultData.Set(ctx, []string{"a"}) fails with 'missing type information; cannot create value' and the response then panics. With the scratch draft fix there are 0 panics across all probe cases, Set succeeds, go test ./function/ passes, and golangci-lint with .golangci.yml reports 0 issues on ./function/. items.title: statestore.NewLockInfo races on a shared math/rand.Rand and can return duplicate lock IDs; use crypto/rand
items.where: statestore/lock_info.go:88-96
items.current: var rngSource = rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano())) (math/rand) is shared package-wide, and generateLockID calls rngSource.Read(buf). A *rand.Rand is not safe for concurrent use. NewLockInfo is a public helper for StateStore.Lock implementations (lock.go:9-12, lock_info.go:43-51), and its docs give no concurrency caveat.
items.replacement: Import crypto/rand instead of math/rand, delete rngSource, and write '_, _ = rand.Read(buf)' (since Go 1.24, crypto/rand.Read never returns an error, always fills the buffer and is safe for concurrent use; go.mod is 1.26 and CI also tests 1.25). Keep uuid.FormatUUID(buf).
items.why_equivalent: This is a bug fix. The ID format does not change: 16 random bytes formatted by uuid.FormatUUID as 8-4-4-4-12 hex. Only the randomness source changes. That is not observable except that the race goes away and IDs stay unique across concurrent calls, including processes started in the same nanosecond.
items.size: about -4/+3 lines (measured on a scratch draft) plus a test (about +25, estimated)
items.risk: low. One behavioural difference worth a line in the PR: crypto/rand.Read terminates the process if the OS RNG fails (legacy Linux without getrandom and without /dev/urandom), whereas math/rand cannot fail; negligible, since go-plugin's TLS setup already depends on crypto/rand.
items.proof: Race reproduced by the verifier (9, 10 and 4 races in three -race runs of 64 goroutines). The duplicate rate did not reproduce at 64 calls (0 of 40 runs); duplicates occur under sustained concurrency: 14-24 per 64,000 IDs (16 goroutines x 4000) and 274-717 per 1.2M IDs (8 x 150,000). With the crypto/rand draft: 0 races, 0 duplicates in 320,000 IDs, go test -race ./statestore/ passes, golangci-lint 0 issues.
items.impact: Data race (go test -race failures in provider suites) and, under sustained concurrent calls, duplicate lock IDs. Duplicates are close to harmless in practice: lock IDs are compared only for the same state, and Terraform serialises Lock calls within a provider process.
notes: Rejected alternative: uuid.GenerateUUID() from go-uuid, which is already a dependency. It returns an error when crypto/rand fails, and with this function shape an error would yield an empty LockID. The StateStore docs (lock.go:34-36) define an empty LockID as 'locking not supported', so locking would be silently disabled.

The math/rand + NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano()) seeding is also an outdated idiom (math/rand is auto-seeded since Go 1.20). Terraform core's statemgr has the same pattern; it was copied, not designed for concurrent library use.

Not a finding, notes only: generateLockInfoWho's function comment ('will return an empty string if any errors are encountered') and its inline comment ('return any information we have') contradict each other and the code. A host error returns the username; a user error returns '' even when the host is known.

items.size: +1 configuration line and about ±12 test lines (estimated)
items.risk: low: contributors must then write current idioms. CI already runs golangci-lint v2 through golangci-lint-action v9.3.0 with no version pin, and modernize ships with golangci-lint v2.
items.proof: Scratch golangci-lint v2.15 run with modernize enabled at 00badb1 (the counts above). Area G confirmed that once every go fix analyzer is applied, go fix reports nothing more.
notes: This is a maintainer decision: the project curates its linter list deliberately. Propose it as its own PR, after the conversions.

protocol: Branch from main; one issue per PR; PR title names the issue ID from this report; no CHANGELOG entry for refactors and test changes (CONTRIBUTING: refactoring does not get an entry), a BUG FIXES changie entry for every bug PR.

Before touching code: run `go test ./<package>/...` for every package the PR touches and record the test list (`go test -run . -v ./pkg 2>&1 | grep -E '^(=== RUN|--- (PASS|FAIL))' | sort`); after the change the list of test IDs and statuses must be identical (test-identity diff), not just the pass count.

`GOTOOLCHAIN=auto go vet ./... && gofmt -s -l . && golangci-lint run ./...` (golangci-lint v2.15+, built with Go 1.26) must stay at 0 issues; forcetypeassert is enforced, so any new type assertion needs `, ok`.

For items that cite go fix: apply exactly one analyzer (`go fix -diff -<analyzer> ./...` to preview, then without -diff), commit, and verify the diff contains only that analyzer's rewrite; never run all analyzers in one PR.

For duplication removals: diff the extracted helper against every copy it replaces (normalise names with sed) before deleting the copies; the report's 'where' field lists every copy; a copy that differs in one line is a separate decision.

For items in internal/fwserver, internal/fwschemadata and internal/reflect: also run `go test ./internal/proto5server/... ./internal/proto6server/...` (they exercise the full RPC path) and, before merging, the terraform-provider-corner acceptance jobs in CI must be green for both protocols.

Public packages: `go doc` output for the package before and after must be identical (exported names, signatures, doc comments); `gorelease`-style API diff is the acceptance criterion for any PR touching a non-internal package.
Bugs: add the failing test first (named in the item), confirm it fails on main, then fix; the test name goes in the changie entry body.
Keep this report's issues.json next to the code review: tick items off by ID so the next audit can diff against it.
